newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russians give valenki footwear the boot.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russians give valenki footwear the boot.

text.p: The Red Army, used to the bitter cold of the Russian winter, wore valenki felt boots to victory in World War Two.

Half a century later traffic police, grandmothers, fishermen, farmers and polar-explorers still swear that only this traditional footwear can properly protect the feet in snow and sub-zero temperatures.
Some enthusiasts even say the clumsy, grey-brown boot has some sort of magic healing power.

But both the boot and the factories which make it are in trouble in the post-Soviet world. Fashion-conscious Russians shun the bulky boot in favour of smarter models and the firms which make it are short of cash.
"Demand has gone down in the last few years," says Tatyana Skyba, director of Moscow's Gorizont factory, which has produced valenki since 1925.
Parts of the plant already look their age. But the rich investor with whom Skyba would like to deal has yet to appear.

The Russian government stopped subsidising valenki production after the collapse of communism and the start of market-oriented economic reforms in 1992 and the factory has been forced to turn to state and private clients for orders.
But they too have been hit by the financial crisis which is crippling the whole of Russian industry. They lack cash to pay their bills and hold back on orders.
And the average Russian consumer who simply had to step into valenki because there was no choice now prefers lighter and more fashionable boots made of leather or synthetics.
"In Moscow you would not see a woman aged between 20 and 50 wearing felt boots," says Zhenya, a 20-year-old Moscow student, who says she would not be caught dead in valenki within city limits.
In Moscow and Russia's second city of St Petersburg valenkis are not sold in footwear shops. But they were on offer at one pet market, where Russian ice fishermen tend to buy their gear.
At the Gorizont factory, output has dropped well below 100,000 pairs from some 300,000 in 1980.
The 100 or so workers, many of them women, can put together up to 500 pairs a day. But they only work during the winter season -- in summer Gorizont shuts down.
The director, who joined the company 35 years ago, says the valenki deserved much better. "It is an ecologically clean product. Nothing but pure water comes into contact with the wool."
In the plant, spread out among several floors in different small buildings, no chemical agents are visible in the production process.
Thick layers of mud-coloured wool swirl around a noisy green machine to thicken the fibres, the first of several steps needed to form a real valenki.
Then the wads of wool are pressed into the shape of a huge boot, more than one metre (three feet) long and big enough for even the biggest fairy-tale giant.
The monster-shoe is then put in warm water and wooden blocks beat and pummel it down to human size, pressing it on metal moulds according to length and width.

There is no difference between right and left boots and the traditionel valenki come without any sole. But Gorizont now adds rubber heels on request, which are generally considered useful while walking in mud and icy slush.
Skyba says valenki can do more than just keep a person's legs warm. The rough texture massages your feet, peels rough skin from the sole of your bare feet and helps against colds and even arthritis.
And they are happy boots, bound to make the wearer happy too, she says. "The wool comes from happy, living sheep and it has a positive energy which is transferred to the wearer."
Some Western companies have shown interest in the Gorizont boots and Russian fashion designer Slava Zaitsev even promoted valenki on the cat-walks in Paris.
But western interest in Russian felt boots has been limited. Skyba says maybe a change in world climate would help in selling the shoes abroad.
But she is not afraid that valenki will die out in their homeland. "There will always be people working outside in the harsh winters."
She said every Russian familiy should rearrange their wardrobes and switch to homemade products. "A Russian household should have several pairs of valenki -- one for each parent, one for each child."
